course.title: Memory Forensics
course.description: A practical, research-driven Memory Forensics course covering volatile evidence, acquisition and integrity, virtual and physical memory, Volatility 3, Windows and Linux analysis, suspicious-memory and YARA triage, credential exposure, timeline reasoning, cross-source correlation, automation, and professional reporting. The course is designed around authorized lab work and emphasizes current authoritative documentation, reproducibility, and honest limitations.
prerequisites: Basic OS concepts: processes, threads, virtual memory, files, and permissions
Comfort with Windows and Linux command lines
Basic networking concepts: IP, TCP/UDP, sockets, and client/server communication
Basic digital-forensics concepts including hashing and evidence integrity
An isolated lab or authorized memory samples
learningOutcomes: Explain why volatile memory is valuable and how acquisition choices affect evidentiary scope.
Explain virtual/physical memory and page-table concepts relevant to forensic interpretation.
Handle authorized Windows and Linux memory images using documented acquisition and integrity procedures.
Install and operate Volatility 3 reproducibly and diagnose common failures.
Analyze Windows and Linux processes, ancestry, command context, memory mappings, modules, and network objects.
Identify suspicious memory indicators without treating heuristics as proof.
Use controlled YARA-oriented scanning and contextualize matches.
Handle credential material and other secrets as sensitive evidence.
Build normalized timelines and correlate memory with independent evidence.
Automate repeatable analysis while preserving raw outputs and failures.
Write professional findings with explicit provenance and limitations.
Complete an end-to-end memory-forensics incident-triage project.

modules.title: Memory Forensics Foundations
modules.description: Understand volatile evidence, memory architecture, acquisition versus analysis, and forensic integrity.

lessons.title: Volatile Evidence and Memory Forensics
lessons.description: Introduces RAM as a changing evidence source and defines the scope of memory forensics.

notes.text: NIST describes RAM as volatile data that can contain frequently or recently accessed information such as data files, password hashes, and recent commands. Memory can also retain residual data in free or slack regions.
A memory image is a snapshot. It does not prove that every byte ever present on the system is represented.

items: High-value artifacts include processes, command context, network state, loaded modules, secrets, and residual data.
Interpretation must include acquisition context and limitations.

notes.text: Do not treat a single memory artifact as self-proving; corroborate important findings.

practicals.title: Volatile triage plan
practicals.description: Design an authorized triage sequence that preserves volatile evidence.
practicals.steps: Record case/time; collect minimally invasive context; acquire memory; hash; preserve; analyze separately.
practicals.solution: A sequence that prioritizes volatile evidence and records every action.

quiz.question: Why is RAM called volatile evidence?
options: It changes while the system runs and may be lost on power removal
It is always more reliable than disk
quiz.answer: It changes while the system runs and may be lost on power removal
quiz.explanation: Volatile data changes during execution and can disappear when power is removed.

lessons.title: Acquisition Versus Analysis
lessons.description: Separates capturing volatile memory from interpreting the resulting image.

notes.text: Volatility 3 is an analysis framework, not a memory acquisition utility. Its Windows tutorial identifies WinPmem and FTK Imager as acquisition examples, while its Linux tutorial points to AVML.
The acquisition method determines what evidence exists for later analysis, so tool version, time, system state, and image type must be recorded.

items: A crash dump is not automatically equivalent to complete physical RAM.
Analysis should normally occur on a verified copy.

notes.text: Only acquire systems or datasets for which you have explicit authorization.

quiz.question: What is Volatility 3 primarily used for?
quiz.answer: Memory-image analysis
quiz.explanation: Volatility 3 interprets memory images through OS-aware plugins and layers.

lessons.title: Virtual and Physical Memory
lessons.description: Builds the address-translation model needed to reason about memory layers and process context.

notes.text: Microsoft explains that processes use virtual address spaces and that page tables translate virtual addresses to physical memory. The resident subset is the process working set.
Volatility 3 uses layers and symbol-aware objects to move from memory bytes toward operating-system structures.

items: A virtual address is meaningful only in an address-space context.
Missing pages or incomplete images can limit reconstruction.

practicals.title: Virtual-to-physical explanation
practicals.description: Explain how a process virtual address reaches physical memory and why an image may not contain the referenced bytes.
practicals.steps: Describe page-table translation, physical frame lookup, and image offset limitations.
practicals.solution: A correct conceptual explanation that does not assume complete page availability.

quiz.question: What do page tables primarily provide?
quiz.answer: Virtual-to-physical address mappings
quiz.explanation: Page tables provide mappings used by hardware for address translation.

tasks.title: Design an evidence-preservation workflow
tasks.problemStatement: A workstation may be shut down soon; specify how to prioritize volatile evidence without unnecessary interaction.
tasks.hint: Treat acquisition, verification, analysis, and reporting as separate phases.
tasks.solutionCode:
steps=['record context','acquire authorized memory','hash image','preserve original','analyze working copy','report limitations']
print('\n'.join(steps))
tasks.solutionExplanation: The workflow separates evidence facts from analyst interpretation.

modules.title: Acquisition, Integrity, and Laboratory Preparation
modules.description: Learn Windows dump scope, Linux AVML acquisition, image validation, and safe lab organization.

lessons.title: Windows Memory Dump Types
lessons.description: Explains complete, kernel, active, and small dump scope.

notes.text: Microsoft documents complete, kernel, small, and active dump types. A complete dump records system memory at crash time; a kernel dump focuses on kernel and kernel-mode memory and omits user-mode application memory.
Dump type therefore constrains what a forensic analyst can conclude.

items: Use complete-memory evidence when user-mode memory is central.
Always state dump scope as a limitation.

practicals.title: Dump-scope matrix
practicals.description: Map four investigation questions to complete or kernel dump scope.
practicals.steps: Identify whether each question requires user-mode or kernel memory; record omissions.
practicals.solution: Questions requiring user-mode evidence generally need a dump containing user-mode memory.

quiz.question: Which Windows dump type is broadest for system-memory questions?
quiz.answer: Complete
quiz.explanation: Microsoft describes a complete memory dump as recording all system memory at crash time.

lessons.title: Linux Acquisition with AVML
lessons.description: Uses the Microsoft AVML project to teach authorized Linux volatile-memory acquisition.

notes.text: AVML is an x86_64 userland Linux volatile-memory acquisition tool written in Rust. Its documented commands include acquire, convert, upload, and stream.
AVML can use supported kernel memory sources; its documentation notes that kernel lockdown can prevent acquisition.

items: Record kernel version, tool version, time, source, output format, and hash.
Acquisition is a live action and can alter system state.

notes.text: Do not collect memory from systems without authorization.

practicals.title: Acquire a Linux lab image
practicals.description: Use AVML on an isolated Linux VM and hash the resulting image.
practicals.steps: Record metadata; run acquire; hash output; preserve manifest.
practicals.solution: A memory image plus SHA-256 and acquisition record.

quiz.question: What is AVML?
quiz.answer: A Linux volatile-memory acquisition tool
quiz.explanation: The Microsoft project identifies AVML as a portable Linux memory-acquisition tool.

lessons.title: Image Validation and Layers
lessons.description: Explains why extensions are insufficient and how Volatility 3 validates images.

notes.text: Volatility 3 describes memory layers as addressable data bodies used to move from a physical representation toward virtual and OS-specific views.
A first Windows validation command is commonly `windows.info`; failures should be diagnosed through image, plugin, dependency, and symbol evidence.

items: File extensions do not guarantee internal structure.
Do not invent a profile when current Volatility 3 cannot identify an image.

quiz.question: Why is a file extension insufficient for memory-format identification?
options: Different acquisition tools can use different internal representations
quiz.answer: Different acquisition tools can use different internal representations
quiz.explanation: The actual image structure and provenance determine interpretation.

tasks.title: Build a cross-platform acquisition checklist
tasks.description: Create one checklist with common forensic controls and platform-specific acquisition steps.
tasks.problemStatement: A team needs Windows and Linux acquisition procedures without pretending the methods are identical.
tasks.hint: Keep common evidence controls identical and acquisition details platform-specific.
tasks.solutionCode:
checklist={'common':['authorization','UTC time','case ID','hash'],'windows':['dump type','build'],'linux':['kernel','AVML version','lockdown']}
print(checklist)
tasks.solutionExplanation: The checklist makes platform differences explicit while preserving common forensic controls.

modules.title: Volatility 3 Architecture and Workflow
modules.description: Install and operate Volatility 3 reproducibly, understand symbols and layers, and troubleshoot failures.

lessons.title: Installation and Versioning
lessons.description: Creates an isolated Volatility 3 environment and records tool provenance.

notes.text: The official Volatility 3 repository documents Python 3.8+ and installation from PyPI. A virtual environment reduces dependency conflicts.
For forensic reproducibility, save the installed version and operating-system details.

items: Do not silently mix Volatility 2 and Volatility 3 syntax.
Use the official repository for installation guidance.

practicals.title: Reproducible installation
practicals.description: Install Volatility 3 in a venv and record version information.
practicals.steps: Create venv; install; run `vol -h`; save package version.

quiz.question: Why use a Python virtual environment for Volatility 3?
options: To isolate dependencies and improve reproducibility
quiz.answer: To isolate dependencies and improve reproducibility
quiz.explanation: Isolation improves reproducibility and dependency control.

lessons.title: Layers, Context, Objects, and Symbols
lessons.description: Explains the architecture behind structured memory interpretation.
learningObjectives: distinguish Windows and Linux symbol workflows

notes.text: Volatility 3 documents memory layers, templates/objects, and symbol tables as central components held in a Context.
Windows symbol retrieval can use PDB-related mechanisms documented by the project; Linux analysis commonly requires suitable ISF symbol files.

items: Symbols must match the target kernel/build.
A symbol failure should be diagnosed, not bypassed with a guessed profile.

quiz.question: What is the primary role of symbols?
options: Describe OS data structures so memory can be interpreted as objects
quiz.answer: Describe OS data structures so memory can be interpreted as objects
quiz.explanation: Symbols connect memory bytes to build-specific structures and fields.

summary: distinguish Windows and Linux symbol workflows

lessons.title: Plugin Discovery and Troubleshooting
lessons.description: Teaches explicit plugin selection, help usage, raw-output preservation, and error classification.

notes.text: The Volatility 3 CLI supports OS-qualified plugin names and warns that short names can be ambiguous across operating systems.
A disciplined workflow captures the exact command, tool version, stdout, stderr, exit status, and relevant symbol/image information.

items: Validate image recognition before debugging higher-level plugins.
One successful plugin does not validate every interpretation.

practicals.title: Troubleshooting decision tree
practicals.description: Build a decision tree for an unavailable or failing plugin.
practicals.steps: Check plugin availability, image validation, symbols, dependencies, and reproduce exact error.
practicals.solution: A decision tree that identifies the failure class before changing settings.

quiz.question: Why prefer `windows.pslist` over ambiguous `pslist`?
options: It explicitly selects the Windows plugin
quiz.answer: It explicitly selects the Windows plugin
quiz.explanation: OS-qualified names reduce ambiguity.

tasks.title: Automate a reproducible first pass
tasks.description: Create a Python wrapper around Volatility 3.
tasks.problemStatement: Run image validation, process listing, and network enumeration while preserving stdout/stderr and not modifying the image.
tasks.hint: Use a subprocess argument list rather than shell=True.
tasks.solutionCode:
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
image=Path('memory.dmp')
for plugin in ['windows.info','windows.pslist','windows.netscan']:
    r=subprocess.run(['vol','-f',str(image),plugin],capture_output=True,text=True,check=False)
    Path(plugin.replace('.','_')+'.stdout.txt').write_text(r.stdout)
    Path(plugin.replace('.','_')+'.stderr.txt').write_text(r.stderr)
tasks.solutionExplanation: The wrapper preserves evidence of both successful and failed plugin execution.

modules.title: Windows Memory Analysis
modules.description: Perform structured Windows analysis from process enumeration through virtual-memory and network correlation.

lessons.title: Process Enumeration: pslist, psscan, pstree
lessons.description: Compares normal process enumeration, scanning, and ancestry.

notes.text: Volatility 3 documents psscan as scanning for process objects in a Windows memory image. pslist and psscan provide complementary views; pstree adds parent-child context.
A process appearing in one view but not another is an investigative lead, not automatic proof of hiding or malware.

items: Compare PID, PPID, name, timestamps, and lifecycle clues.
Record hypotheses separately from observations.

practicals.title: Process-view comparison
practicals.description: Compare pslist, psscan, and pstree on an authorized sample.
practicals.steps: Run all three; normalize PID/PPID/name/time; inspect discrepancies.
practicals.solution: A process comparison with explicit hypotheses and limitations.

quiz.question: What is the value of comparing pslist and psscan?
quiz.answer: It provides complementary enumeration views
quiz.explanation: Different enumeration methods can expose discrepancies requiring investigation.

lessons.title: Command Lines, DLLs, and Handles
lessons.description: Builds process context from execution arguments, loaded modules, and OS-managed handles.

notes.text: Command lines can reveal script paths and arguments. DLL lists show loaded modules, while handles can expose relationships to files, registry keys, mutexes, pipes, and other objects.
A suspicious module or handle becomes more meaningful when correlated with process ancestry, memory permissions, and network state.

items: Do not judge a process from its name alone.
Record paths and object types precisely.

quiz.question: Which provides stronger context for an unusual DLL?
options: Path plus process, ancestry, and memory context
quiz.answer: Path plus process, ancestry, and memory context
quiz.explanation: Context reduces false positives.

lessons.title: VADs, Injection Indicators, and netscan
lessons.description: Uses virtual-memory regions and network objects to prioritize suspicious processes.

notes.text: Windows virtual-memory regions can be examined through VAD-oriented plugins such as `windows.vadinfo` and `windows.vadwalk`. Executable private memory can be a useful indicator but is not proof of injection.
`windows.netscan` scans for network objects and can provide process context that helps connect memory evidence to network activity.

items: Use multiple independent artifact classes before escalating a hypothesis.
Network state is time-specific and may be incomplete.

notes.text: Never execute extracted suspicious code merely to validate a hypothesis.

practicals.title: Network-to-process correlation
practicals.description: Trace a network object to process, command, and module context.
practicals.steps: Run netscan; select PID; inspect process and command context; record endpoints and time.
practicals.solution: A network finding supported by process context.

quiz.question: Does executable private memory prove injection?
options: No, it is an indicator requiring context
quiz.answer: No, it is an indicator requiring context
quiz.explanation: Legitimate software can create executable private memory.

tasks.title: Build a Windows process-investigation report
tasks.description: Correlate process, command, module, VAD, and network artifacts.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce a shortlist of processes for escalation from an authorized image without relying on names alone.
tasks.hint: Use PID as a join key, then validate timestamps and context.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The structure keeps multiple artifact classes attached to a process identifier.

modules.title: Linux Memory Analysis
modules.description: Analyze Linux process state, memory mappings, command history, modules, sockets, and process-memory access indicators.

lessons.title: Linux /proc and Memory Maps
lessons.description: Connects Linux /proc semantics to memory-forensics concepts.

notes.text: Linux kernel documentation describes `/proc/<pid>/maps` as current mapped memory regions and permissions, `/proc/<pid>/mem` as process memory, and `/proc/<pid>/pagemap` as page-table information.
Live /proc output can be racy because mappings change while being read; a memory image is a historical snapshot.

items: Classify code, heap, stack, shared libraries, and anonymous mappings.
Kernel-version semantics can change, so consult matching documentation.

practicals.title: Classify a Linux memory map
practicals.description: Inspect a benign process map and classify regions by permission and backing.
practicals.steps: Read maps; classify code/heap/stack/shared/anonymous; explain forensic significance.

quiz.question: What does `/proc/<pid>/maps` describe?
quiz.answer: Mapped memory regions and permissions
quiz.explanation: That is its documented purpose.

lessons.title: Linux Process Enumeration and Ancestry
lessons.description: Uses pslist, psscan, and pstree to reconstruct process state.

notes.text: The Volatility Linux tutorial identifies process-listing and scanning plugins and notes broad Linux plugin coverage.
Process discrepancies are investigation leads and should be correlated with command, module, socket, and mapping evidence.

items: Process names alone are weak evidence.
Record PID/PPID and available timestamps.

quiz.question: Why compare Linux process views?
options: To obtain complementary evidence and identify discrepancies
quiz.answer: To obtain complementary evidence and identify discrepancies
quiz.explanation: Different views provide different evidence.

lessons.title: Bash History, Modules, and Sockets
lessons.description: Combines command history, kernel modules, and socket state for Linux investigations.

notes.text: Volatility 3 documents `linux.bash` for recovering bash history and lists `linux.lsmod` and `linux.sockstat` among representative Linux plugins.

MITRE's Linux credential-access detection strategy emphasizes monitoring access to `/proc/<pid>/mem` or `/proc/<pid>/maps` in suspicious contexts; memory analysis can provide supporting context but may need endpoint telemetry.

items: A recovered command is not guaranteed complete history.
An unfamiliar module requires kernel/package provenance checks.

practicals.title: Test a Linux process-memory hypothesis
practicals.description: Evaluate a hypothesis that one process accessed another process's memory.
practicals.steps: Collect process, privilege, command, and memory-access context; compare with independent telemetry where available.
practicals.solution: A supported, weakened, or unresolved hypothesis rather than an automatic verdict.

quiz.question: What is recovered bash history?
options: Potential historical evidence that may be incomplete
quiz.answer: Potential historical evidence that may be incomplete
quiz.explanation: Memory-based recovery can be incomplete.

tasks.title: Investigate Linux process-memory access
tasks.description: Evaluate a suspected unauthorized process-memory access event.
tasks.problemStatement: Use an authorized Linux image to assess whether the evidence is consistent with suspicious /proc access.
tasks.hint: MITRE emphasizes /proc memory access combined with process and privilege context.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task emphasizes defensive detection rather than credential extraction.

modules.title: Malware Hunting, YARA, and Sensitive Memory
modules.description: Use memory heuristics and signature scanning safely and handle credential material defensively.

lessons.title: Malware Indicators and Heuristics
lessons.description: Explains suspicious processes, mappings, modules, and network relationships as leads.

notes.text: Memory malware triage often combines process ancestry, executable private memory, unusual modules, network state, and object relationships.
Each indicator can have benign explanations, so confidence should increase only when independent evidence aligns.

items: Heuristics prioritize investigation.
Alternative explanations belong in the report.

notes.text: Never describe a heuristic as proof without corroboration.

practicals.title: Indicator-priority worksheet
practicals.description: Create a qualitative triage score using several independent indicators.
practicals.steps: List indicators; assign low/medium/high priority; require corroboration before escalation; document false positives.
practicals.solution: A prioritization aid, not a probability model.

quiz.question: Why can executable private memory be a false positive?
options: Legitimate applications can allocate executable private memory
quiz.answer: Legitimate applications can allocate executable private memory
quiz.explanation: Memory permissions have legitimate uses.

lessons.title: malfind and Suspicious User-Mode Memory
lessons.description: Uses malfind-oriented analysis while emphasizing limitations.

notes.text: The Volatility project describes malfind as helping identify hidden or injected user-mode code/DLLs using characteristics such as VAD information and page permissions.
Different injection techniques and legitimate executable allocations mean malfind output requires contextual validation.

items: Preserve extracted bytes as evidence; do not execute them on a production system.
Compare with module lists and memory-region context.

quiz.question: What is malfind designed to help locate?
options: Potential hidden/injected user-mode code or DLL regions
quiz.answer: Potential hidden/injected user-mode code or DLL regions
quiz.explanation: That is the plugin's intended purpose.

lessons.title: YARA Scanning and Credential Exposure
lessons.description: Teaches controlled YARA memory scanning and safe handling of secrets recovered from RAM.

notes.text: YARA provides a rule language for pattern matching. Volatility 3 has YARA-oriented plugins when the necessary dependency is available. A YARA match is not proof of malware.
NIST notes that RAM can contain password hashes and recent commands; MITRE documents credential-dumping techniques involving memory and Linux /proc access.

items: Never paste real credentials into reports or training notes.
Record the minimum necessary locator/context and trigger defensive response when appropriate.

notes.text: Only analyze credential material from authorized evidence and never reuse recovered secrets.

practicals.title: Benign YARA memory scan
practicals.description: Create a unique training-marker rule and scan a controlled sample.
practicals.steps: Write rule; validate syntax; scan; record address/PID/context.
practicals.solution: Only the controlled marker should match in the designed sample.

quiz.question: What does a YARA match establish?
options: Only that the rule matched its condition
That the rule is always correct
quiz.answer: Only that the rule matched its condition
quiz.explanation: YARA establishes a pattern match; context determines meaning.

tasks.title: Build a defensive memory-hunting playbook
tasks.description: Combine process, VAD, network, YARA, and sensitive-memory indicators.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a safe workflow for an authorized endpoint image without executing recovered code or reusing secrets.
tasks.hint: Start broad, narrow to high-priority processes, then scan targeted regions.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The playbook is evidence-driven and avoids unsafe execution.

modules.title: Timeline, Correlation, Automation, and Reporting
modules.description: Turn plugin output into reproducible investigative findings and a professional report.

lessons.title: Temporal Reasoning and Timelines
lessons.description: Builds timelines from memory timestamps while separating event and acquisition time.

notes.text: Memory artifacts may contain process, network, and other timestamps. Acquisition time is separate from event time. Clock drift and timezone assumptions can affect interpretation.

items: Record source plugin and artifact for every timestamp.
Do not invent precision not supported by the evidence.

practicals.title: Normalized timeline
practicals.description: Create a UTC timeline from three hypothetical memory artifacts with source and confidence.
practicals.steps: Normalize times; add event/source/object; sort; state limitations.

quiz.question: Which timestamp should order an event?
options: Reliable artifact event time, with acquisition time recorded separately
quiz.answer: Reliable artifact event time, with acquisition time recorded separately
quiz.explanation: Event time and acquisition time answer different questions.

lessons.title: Cross-Source Correlation
lessons.description: Correlates memory with disk, network, and endpoint telemetry.

notes.text: Memory findings become stronger when independent evidence such as endpoint process events, disk artifacts, DNS, firewall, or packet data supports the same event.
Repeating a parser is not the same as independent corroboration.

items: Document contradictions instead of hiding them.
Use source provenance in every finding.

quiz.question: Why is independent corroboration valuable?
options: It can validate or challenge a single-source interpretation
quiz.answer: It can validate or challenge a single-source interpretation
quiz.explanation: Independent sources reduce overreliance on one artifact.

lessons.title: Automation, Performance, and Reporting
lessons.description: Automates repeatable analysis while preserving failures and produces precise forensic findings.

notes.text: Large memory images are I/O intensive. Running every plugin blindly can create low-value output and resource contention. Volatility 3 exposes configuration and parallelism controls.
A professional finding separates observation, interpretation, corroboration, conclusion, and limitation.

items: Preserve stdout, stderr, exit code, command, and tool version.
Use targeted plugins after broad triage.

notes.text: Do not hide failed plugins or silently replace unsupported results.

practicals.title: Failure-aware analysis manifest
practicals.description: Design a batch runner that records each plugin's output, error, exit code, and timestamp.
practicals.steps: Run independent plugins; continue after failure; write deterministic filenames and a JSON manifest.
practicals.solution: A complete run manifest including failed plugins.

quiz.question: Which finding style is most defensible?
options: The image contains an unusual process and network object consistent with the hypothesis, requiring corroboration
The IP is malicious because it appears in memory
quiz.answer: The image contains an unusual process and network object consistent with the hypothesis, requiring corroboration
quiz.explanation: The statement separates observed evidence from interpretation and avoids overclaiming.

tasks.title: Produce a complete memory-forensics report
tasks.description: Create a reproducible case report from an authorized image.
tasks.problemStatement: Document provenance, validation, process/network findings, suspicious-memory indicators, timeline, and limitations.
tasks.hint: Use question → artifact → output → correlation → conclusion → limitation.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The structure makes each conclusion traceable.

modules.title: Final Real-World Project: Memory Forensics Incident Triage
modules.description: Apply the complete course workflow to an authorized memory image and produce a reproducible forensic evidence package.

lessons.title: Project Brief and Assessment
lessons.description: Defines the final assessment and quality criteria.

notes.text: The project is assessed on evidence quality and reasoning, not plugin count. Every major conclusion must be traceable to raw output and evidence metadata.

items: No unauthorized collection.
No execution of extracted suspicious code.
No reuse or publication of recovered secrets.
Unsupported plugins and failures must be documented.

quiz.question: What is the primary project success criterion?
options: A reproducible evidence-backed investigation with accurate limitations
quiz.answer: A reproducible evidence-backed investigation with accurate limitations
quiz.explanation: Forensic competence is measured by defensible reasoning and reproducibility.

project.name: Memory Forensics Incident Triage and Evidence Report
project.description: An end-to-end authorized investigation that validates a memory image, performs platform-specific Volatility 3 triage, correlates process/network/memory indicators, handles sensitive memory safely, builds a timeline, automates repeatable runs, and produces a defensible report.
steps: Select an authorized Windows or Linux training image and record provenance, size, SHA-256, acquisition time, and source.
Create a Python virtual environment, install Volatility 3, and record the version.
Validate the image and document OS/build and symbol context.
Run broad process and network enumeration, then select high-priority processes using observable evidence.
Perform platform-specific deep analysis such as DLLs/handles/VAD/malfind on Windows or bash/modules/sockets/maps on Linux where supported.
Preserve command lines, stdout, stderr, exit codes, and analysis timestamps.
Handle credential material as sensitive evidence; never publish or reuse recovered secrets.
Build a UTC-normalized timeline and correlate with independent telemetry when available.
Write findings as observation → interpretation → corroboration → conclusion → limitation.
Recalculate the memory-image hash and verify it matches the original manifest.
Package the report and run manifest without modifying the original evidence.

code.README.md:
Memory Forensics Incident Triage

Use only with authorized evidence. Requires Python 3.8+ and Volatility 3 installed as `vol`.

Example: `python memory_triage.py --image /path/to/memory.dmp --platform windows --out results`
code.memory_triage.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import argparse, hashlib, json, shutil, subprocess

PLUGINS = {
    "windows": ["windows.info","windows.pslist","windows.psscan","windows.pstree","windows.cmdline","windows.netscan"],
    "linux": ["linux.pslist","linux.psscan","linux.pstree","linux.bash","linux.lsmod","linux.sockstat"],
}

def sha256_file(path):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(1024 * 1024), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()

def run_plugin(image, plugin, out):
    name = plugin.replace(".", "_")
    cmd = ["vol", "-f", str(image), plugin]
    start = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=False)
    stdout = out / f"{name}.stdout.txt"
    stderr = out / f"{name}.stderr.txt"
    stdout.write_text(result.stdout, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
    stderr.write_text(result.stderr, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
    return {"plugin": plugin, "command": cmd, "started_utc": start,
            "finished_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
            "returncode": result.returncode, "stdout": str(stdout), "stderr": str(stderr)}

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--image", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--platform", choices=PLUGINS, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--out", default="memory-results")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    image = Path(args.image).expanduser().resolve()
    out = Path(args.out).expanduser().resolve()
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    if not image.is_file():
        raise SystemExit(f"Memory image not found: {image}")
    if not shutil.which("vol"):
        raise SystemExit("Volatility 3 'vol' is not in PATH")

    manifest = {
        "created_utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        "image": str(image),
        "size_bytes": image.stat().st_size,
        "sha256_before": sha256_file(image),
        "platform": args.platform,
        "runs": []
    }

    for plugin in PLUGINS[args.platform]:
        manifest["runs"].append(run_plugin(image, plugin, out))

    manifest["sha256_after"] = sha256_file(image)
    manifest["image_unchanged"] = manifest["sha256_before"] == manifest["sha256_after"]

    (out / "run-manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

    if not manifest["image_unchanged"]:
        raise SystemExit("Evidence image hash changed during analysis")
    print(f"Analysis complete: {out / 'run-manifest.json'}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
